rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate the elution window and critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. A midrange temperature leaves room to probe temperature-dependent selectivity in either direction.

Only the first pair limits the score, while all peaks elute comfortably before 10 minutes. Change temperature alone to test whether selectivity resolves that pair without sacrificing the time advantage.

Keep the favorable temperature and make the gradient slightly shallower to improve the first pair from R = 1.41 toward full resolution. The last peak has ample margin below 10 minutes, so this change could reach the maximum CRF of 1.0.

Injection 3 reached the maximum CRF; now test a faster fully resolved method. This gradient slope lies between injections 2 and 3 and should retain R ≥ 1.5 for the first pair while shortening the last-peak time.

Raise the starting organic fraction one step to shorten retention while slightly reducing gradient steepness. Test whether this preserves full resolution of the first pair and improves on injection 4’s last-peak time.

Restore the lower starting organic fraction and test a slope between injections 2 and 4, targeting just enough resolution for the first pair. The last peak may elute briefly into the final hold; this tests whether the shorter gradient preserves maximum CRF with a shorter last-peak time.

With maximum CRF already secured, explore a cooler, steeper gradient for a potentially faster fully resolved method. Lower temperature may separate the first pair on the opposite side of a selectivity crossover, while the steeper gradient offsets increased retention.

Raise temperature one step to split the late three-peak cluster seen at 25 C while testing whether the first pair remains fully resolved. Keeping the gradient unchanged isolates the temperature effect on these competing critical pairs.

Test a shifted gradient window to disrupt the late three-peak co-elution at 25 C and shorten retention. The first pair had resolution to spare at this temperature, allowing a higher starting organic fraction to be explored.

Test whether moderate warming separates the late cluster while a shallower gradient preserves the early pair’s resolution. This explores an alternative fully resolved method at a lower temperature, with the maximum-score 60 C methods already secured.

Test a higher starting organic fraction and shorter gradient at 35 C to reduce the last-peak time. This probes whether the shifted window improves early-pair selectivity enough to offset gradient compression while retaining separation of the late cluster.

Return to the successful 60 C region and test a slightly steeper slope than injection 6. This probes the resolution boundary for the first pair and may shorten the last-peak time while preserving maximum CRF.

Reduce the endpoint by one step relative to injection 5 to recover the first pair’s small resolution deficit. This tests a narrower-window alternative expected to retain all eight peaks below 10 minutes and potentially reach maximum CRF.

Use a slope slightly shallower than injection 6 and an endpoint high enough for every peak to elute during the gradient. This targets maximum CRF with a little more resolution margin than injection 6 and a last-peak time near seven minutes.

Test a cooler alternative: 30 C favors the early pair, while a shallower gradient should improve separation of the late cluster. The higher starting organic fraction should help keep the last peak below 10 minutes.

Lengthen injection 10’s gradient by one step to address its sole unresolved pair, which had R = 1.34. This tests whether a second temperature region can achieve maximum CRF while keeping the last peak below 10 minutes.

The maximum CRF is already secured; test a more robust maximum-score method by increasing resolution margin while keeping the last peak below 10 minutes. Monitor both the first pair and the third–fourth pair, whose resolution decreases with shallower gradients at 60 C.

Shorten injection 17 by one gradient step to reduce analysis time while retaining a larger resolution margin than the fastest methods. This should balance the first pair, which benefits from shallower gradients, against the third–fourth pair, which benefits from steeper gradients.

Slightly steepen the effective slope relative to injection 13 while retaining its starting composition and temperature. This tests whether its small resolution margin permits a shorter last-peak time without losing maximum CRF.

Test one temperature step below injection 17 to assess whether full resolution survives a modest temperature change. Its resolution and time margins make this a plausible lower-temperature method with maximum CRF.

Test whether a higher starting organic fraction paired with a shallower gradient can preserve full resolution at 60 C. This extends the successful window-trimming experiments while leaving enough final organic strength to elute all compounds.

Return to a proven starting composition and lengthen injection 19’s gradient one step to give its borderline first pair more resolution margin. This targets maximum CRF with a shorter last-peak time than the robust method from injection 18.

Trim injection 3’s gradient endpoint while preserving its successful slope, starting composition, and temperature. All peaks should elute before the gradient ends, retaining maximum CRF with a shorter programmed gradient.

Trim the endpoint of the well-resolved region near injection 18 while using a slightly steeper slope to shorten retention. This targets maximum CRF with greater resolution margin than the fastest method and all peaks eluting during the gradient.

Use the final injection to shorten retention relative to injection 24 while preserving a useful resolution margin. This slope lies between two fully resolved methods, so maximum CRF is expected; injection 6 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-score method.
